When the time for war comes, no warrior of Tzeentch shall fall beside him without the Breath of Life lifting them from their knees, imbuing them with the strength to raise their blades against the enemies of fate once more.

It is said that Tzeentch once shattered into ten thousand pieces, each shard shifting to form a spell or incantation. Thus, the Blue Scribes ride their Disc of Tzeentch through realms eternal and mortal, squabbling as they seek lost fragments of their god to bind with parchment and ink. Their mission often draws them towards the tumult of battle, where the most destructive and powerful magics are used. If threatened, one of the scribes starts reading at random from the scrolls they have accumulated, trusting the hand of fate – his master – to guide him to a fitting spell for each occasion. With such powerful magics reeled off at random, a foe is as likely to be struck by multicoloured lightning as he is to be drenched by his own personal thunderstorm or transmuted into solid gold.

The Changeling personifies the part of Tzeentch’s psyche that is the meddler, the deceiver, the trickster. He can take the form of other beings, from the tiniest of insects to the most massive of Greater Daemons. None, save for perhaps Tzeentch himself, know the Changeling’s true form, for he goes cowled and cloaked when in his own shape – perhaps even the Changeling himself has forgotten it. That so many of his pranks have caused terrible wars is no concern to him, for he loves the discord of conflict to breed more opportunities to deceive and dismay. When battle begins, the Changeling is wont to adopt the shape and skill of his foes, in turn pounding them to pieces with malicious enthusiasm and borrowed muscle.

Beastmen are creatures of pure Chaos, and so tend to exalt all four Ruinous Powers equally. However, sometimes a she-gor spawns a whelp that is clearly a chosen one of the Changer of Ways, its fur patterned with the Mark of Tzeentch, or its horns curling to form His unholy symbol. These Centigors are as bitter and spiteful as their non-Tzeentchian kin, with a stronger resentment for their own clumsy, awkward nature, and harbouring a deep jealousy of creatures whose minds and bodies are better matched. This feeds their arcane rage and makes them much more dangerous – having been touched by Tzeentch, this is likely no coincidence.

Though undoubtedly savage and monstrous, the Tzaangors are elevated above their ordinary beastkin, having dedicated themselves to Tzeentch in exchange for his darkest blessings. Evolved with a keen, if cruel, intellect, their God has granted them attunement with the arcane, allowing their strength to grow in tandem with any spellcasting that surrounds them. Shrieking and emitting shrill war calls, they fall upon every foe in a flurried rush of blades and vicious stabs, impaling their victims with savage horns. No creature is more eager to impress their duplicitous God. Thus, empowered by magic, the Tzaangors fight with lunatic energies, hoping to earn further mutations in their quest for Change.

The Cockatrice is a deadly, magical beast known to petrify those that look directly into its gaze. Said to dwell in the Annulii Mountains of Ulthuan, Cockatrices are vicious beasts obviously tainted by Chaos for both their unnatural appearance and their fierce disposition in battle. In truth, the Cockatrice is not a bold fighter and prefers to lurk around the fringes of a battlefield where it can safely feast on the dead and dying. Despite the beast's inclination for self-preservation, only a very foolish warrior will attempt to corner one, because when the beast is desperate, it goes berserk, shrinking and clawing at all who approach it with maddened ferocity that more than compensates for its inner cowardice.

A Mutalith Vortex Beast is an utter abomination of nature. A terrifying fusion of monster and magic, the creature has been twisted beyond all reason by the powers of Chaos. Wherever a Mutalith treads, mutation and madness are left in their wake. With a ball of raw magic anchored into the creature’s body, it exemplifies the tumultuous nature of change, as the seething orb of Chaos energy warps and twists everything in its path. The flesh of the Mutalith itself is forever being healed and remoulded, sucked in and poured back out again by the vortex. All the while, these same wisps of malign energy reach out across the battlefield, mutating everything they touch.

Created by Dwarf Master Engineer, Malakai Makaisson, the Goblin Hewer is an ingenious and deadly weapon of war built from only the sturdiest materials. It is a complex machine with a simple purpose, using hydraulic systems to launch axes with lightning speed to trap the unfortunate foe in a deadly storm of metal. Once a terrifying array of axes has been loaded into the contraption, they are released in a whirling barrage of death that can slice through enemy lines with ease. While allies describe the weapon as a "rapid-firing axe-throwing extravaganza of destruction", the enemy describe it only as "certain death".

For five generations, the Slayer Kings of Karak Kadrin laboured under dual vows. But then the son of Ungrim, Garagrim Ironfist, committed to the life of a Slayer by leaving his father's court to live amongst the hard stone halls of the Shrine of Grimnir. Embracing his sacred duties with relish, Garagrim tends the shrine and the temple's store of ancient rune-axes left as tribute by Slayers making a pilgrimage to Karak Kadrin. Though none among them match his own devastating weapons. Chained to Garagrim's wrists so he will never lose them, his twin axes were gifted to him by his father on his coming-of-age. Inscribed by a Grudge Rune and the Master Rune of Skalf Blackhammer, each axe is a statement of deadly intent, and a warning to all of Garagrim's enemies.

Once a prodigiously gifted engineer of the renowned Engineers' Guild, Malakai Makaisson now serves as a Slayer, bearing the shame of a tumultuous and tragic past. As the creator of the Ironclad [[i]]Unsinkable[[/i]] and the Airship [[i]]Indestructible[[/i]] – which both malfunctioned with devastating results – he carries the weight of numerous Dwarfs' deaths on his shoulders, resulting in his ejection from the Engineers' Guild. In the wake of the tragedies, Makaisson took the Slayer Oath, though his days of tinkering and invention are not yet behind him. He continues his craft, building wonders such as the Spirit of Grungni and the infamous Goblin Hewer, in the hopes that one day his shame will be expunged in either triumph or glorious death.

By dint of constant fighting, some Slayers fail more than others at the task of dying in battle, becoming ever more scar-riddled and dangerous over time. Often known as Dragon or Daemon Slayers, they tend to be joined by a swarm of younger brethren from the Slayer Cult who flock towards such renowned killers, assured that a greater Slayer can always lead them straight towards foes against whom a worthy end might be made. This attraction is not altogether appreciated by the irascible and laconic Dragon or Daemon Slayer, who do not want to dare chance one of their following getting in a lucky stroke and robbing them of a glorious final blow.

Having sworn the sacred Slayer Oath, Doomseekers are honour-bound to never retreat from a fight, an unbreakable force that ploughs recklessly into the enemy while whirling their weapons madly around their heads. These Dwarfs are crazed, even by Slayer standards, giving them even more destructive and extreme capabilities. Armed with axes attached to lengths of chain, any foe unfortunate enough to stand in their way is cut down with devastating ferocity, and those who survive are often left with fewer limbs than they started with!

While any seafaring Slayer would claim some association with the infamous captain-turned-pirate of Barak Varr [[i]]Long Drong[[/i]] – the most renowned Dwarf Slayer Pirate in history – some Slayers take to the seas simply because they consider it an easy means to glorious battles. After all, raiding the treasure hoards of notorious pirates and corsairs quickly earns enemies baying for one’s blood – what more can a Slayer ask for? Slayer Pirates are often seen joining the ranks of mercenary companies from Tilea to the Empire, yet in truth their mercenary work is just to keep them in the rum and blackpowder. Their true focus, which has them sail to all corners of the world, is fighting sea monsters!

The Dwarf Thunderbarge class of lighter-than-air warships hasn't quite been perfected yet, but that doesn't stop a few intrepid Dwarf Engineers from taking them to the skies. The bomb racks, cannons and swivel guns of these amazing flying machines can wreak devastation on any enemy battleline. Fortunately for enemies of the Dwarfs, few Thunderbarges have ever been constructed and it is hard to find Engineers insane or inebriated enough to fly such dangerous constructions. In fact, it is not unheard of for the warships to stow a few barrels of Bugman’s aboard to give the crew an extra dosage of courage when needed!

The Order of the Black Rose was founded during the dark days of the Black Plague, its longstanding association with the Cult of Morr signified by the emblazonments across its Knights' armour and barding. Justly famed throughout the land, recruitment of their elite Knightly ranks is drawn from the best warriors of the nation, a great honour which sees them outstandingly equipped at Imperial expense. Their cuirasses are often stained black, as are the heavy weapons and shields they carry, yet it is the prominent imagery of death upon them that makes them a most intimidating adversary on the battlefield.

For three generations the name of Elspeth von Draken, Magisterix of the Amethyst College and Arch-Wizard of the Lore of Death, has been spoken of in hushed tones in the reeking tavern gutters and vaulted noble halls of Nuln alike. An obsessive experimenter and mystic, Elspeth goes where she will, collecting and collating a storehouse of mystical artefacts and lore, which she guards jealously. Surrounded by all manner of occult items, Elspeth has become so saturated with the force of Shyish – the Amethyst Wind of Death – that there are some who whisper she is no longer human at all. To her enemies, Elspeth seems to stand halfway between life and death, a violent spectre in human form whose magic destroys all it touches.

The individuals skilled and eccentric enough to earn the position of Imperial Engineer are obsessed with designing new machines and technological marvels, eager to watch their contraptions tear through the enemies of the Empire. However it is not just their positions as inventors and suppliers of deadly weapons that make Engineers valuable on the battlefield. While not soldiers, they are still part of the Emperor's armed forces, and can often be found taking advantage of 'battlefield conditions' to snipe at the enemy with a variety of powerful experimental rifles and handguns.

Known as the Hound of Judgement, Theodore Bruckner serves as the First Headsman of Nuln and champion of the Countess Emmanuelle. Towering head and shoulders over the majority of Nuln's citizenry, most regard him with abject terror, for he is the personification of bloody-handed justice and death incarnate to the Countess' political enemies. Both savage and skilled, he is famed most for his prodigious – some say inhuman – strength. Gossip surrounding Bruckner's physical prowess became the stuff of legend following his judicial duel with the noted swordsman Lord Hanz Kraster, during which he grappled his plate-armoured opponent, lifting him and aloft and snapping his back with his bare hands!

The soaring eagle is symbol of the golden Wind of Chamon, and is considered by outsiders as a representation of the Gold Wizard’s assumed superiority over their fellow men. In truth, Gold Wizards are aloof in the extreme and the powers they wield on the battlefield do little to dispel such beliefs. It is speculated that they indulge in intellectual vanity to compensate for their often-marred physiques, as constant tinkering with acids and molten metals has left some students of Chamon scarred, burned or mutilated, leaving only their minds with any claim to perfection. Those who successfully unlock Chamon’s secrets, however, do so with frightening results, learning the ways of transmutation to warp armour and weapons to ensure victory for their sides.

Master Engineer Leon Todmeister is credited with creating this modified Hochland hunting rifle, brandished by the exceptional Marksmen of the Imperial Army. Originally dubbed Leon Todmeister's Fantabulously Far-reaching Harquebus of Unforeseeable and Unperceived Bereavement, it was said that he could put a hole in a gold coin at 400 yards. It was also said, however, that Leon's assistant had a bag of pre-holed coins with him at all times. Whatever the truth may be, none can doubt this rifle's deadly efficiency, nor the elite training of the Marksmen that wield it in defence of their homeland.

One of the most lauded institutions in Nuln is the Imperial Gunnery School, a College of Engineers rivalled in the Empire only by that of Altdorf and operators of the largest cannon-foundries anywhere west of the World's Edge Mountains, save for the Dwarfs’. Apprentices and military men from across the Empire and beyond are drawn to study at the Gunnery School, many of whom make their way into its ‘Iron Companies’, that operate as its armed wing. Most numerous among these are the Ironsides, regiments of handgunners consisting of apprentices and retainers who are fitted out in a panoply of black-iron plate armour, reflecting the wealth and status of their patrons.

The troops and War Machines subject to Elspeth’s dark touch are feared as dangerous enigmas even amongst other Imperial regiments, using the forbidden energies of Shyish to bring macabre ends to the Empire’s enemies.

Designed by Gunnery School Engineer, Hezekiah Guttman, the Marienburg Land Ship was proposed as a whimsical boat-shaped alternative to a Steam Tank. As much a project of vanity as one of defence, the end product was a grotesquely-sized, hulking contraption of war, dubbed "The Wonder of the Age" by the provost-marshal of the Imperial Gunnery School. Hastily mimicked designs later commissioned by Imperial forces never quite matched the awesome firepower of the first Land Ship, though it has not stopped them rolling to war when their great expense can be spared. Traversing battlefields on huge, sturdy wheels, Land Ships dwarf the men that fight beside them, providing devastating firepower for the Imperial war effort.

The Masters of the Imperial School of Engineers constantly design new experimental weapons systems with which to outfit the Empire’s Steam Tanks. One such modification incorporates a modified steam-powered version of the highly successful but notoriously unpredictable Helblaster Volley Gun, replacing the standard steam-powered cannons. This has proved to be devastating, often as much to the Engineer himself as to the enemy, and is particularly effective against well-armoured targets. Some of the older School of Engineering members oppose their use, for they see the mounting of Volley Guns on Steam Tanks as far too great a risk. However, these fears are generally outweighed, for the destructive potential of the weapon is formidable by any measure.

Karanak is the three-headed Flesh Hound that prowls Khorne’s grand throne room. He never sleeps, for like the Blood God’s unreasoning vengeance Karanak is ever watchful. Each of his heads tracks his quarry in a different fashion: The first head can follow the trail through physical space, tracking the victim over plains, forests, mountains, and all environments too bizarre to describe. The second can follow the scent through time, back into the past to the very creation of everything that is, or forward to the end of the universe. The third head tracks the quarry via its own thoughts, pursuing through dreamscapes and delusions. Of the three heads it is the last that is most dangerous, for the other two can be fooled by those with the wit to do so, but only the insane can run beyond the trace of their own mind.

Chaos Knights are feared throughout the Old World and beyond as towering, merciless butchers capable of turning the course of battle with a single charge. Yet some of those marked by Nurgle bear an even more striking countenance. Disfigured by disease, the Plaguelord's Rot Knights ride into battle atop vomitous Rot Beasts – the most rabid of Chaos Warhounds that have been plagued and corrupted by Nurgle to become enlarged, slavering mounts whose bites hideously infect those unfortunate enough to survive their encounters with them. Upon these horrible creatures, Rot Knights revel in spreading Nurgle’s maladies at the tip of a sepsis-inducing lance.

Old and beaten down by time, Grukmur is a Bray-Shaman born of the most wild and terrible magic. Countless scars have made a tarnished canvas of his skin, marking him as a surviving veteran of more battles than he ever hoped to a be part of. Such endless tribulations have left him drained by fear and the weariness of ages, yet Grukmur once again finds himself dragged into combat by the braying of his kin. They march to war on the sweet promise of slaughter and meat, and if Grukmur hopes to avoid the ire of his betters, he has no choice but to rush into battle beside them.

Nurgle’s Champions include some of the most foul and disgusting of all Chaos Lords. They are grim individuals, wholeheartedly believing their only sources of fulfilment to be little more than suffering, sickness and war – preferably all at once! Their heavy suits of armour often conceal heavily-diseased forms, yet with Nurgle’s blessings they command His hosts with otherworldly strength and resilience, fearlessly wading into the horrors of battle, bloodthirsty and plague-ridden. It is a Lord of Nurgle’s belief that to attain true understanding of themselves and the world, they must cast aside all the trappings and delusions of life to promote Nurgle’s truth: all is despair!

Epidemius is Nurgle's chosen Tallyman, one of the seven Proctors of Pestilence, and the cataloguer of all the Plaguelord's myriad diseases. His path through the realms is an unpredictable one, for he goes wherever the spoor of pestilence leads him. Epidemius is busiest of all when Nurgle's power is strong, for the might of the Plaguelord is inextricably linked to the constantly shifting ebb and flow of disease. Campaigning armies, with all the poor hygiene that that entails, offer a glut of work for the Tallyman, but also present rare opportunities for his more unusual studies; it is a rare privilege to observe a mortal's decline as their body and soul is ravaged by disease, but the experience is often over far too quickly. Fortunately there are always more victims to study...

Some tales told in bawdy taverns, or recounted amid frightened whispers in small towns, describe {{tr:land_units_onscreen_name_wh3_dlc25_nur_cha_exalted_hero_chieftain}} as the personification of Chaos itself. Gripped by delirium and madness, this distinguished Warrior of Chaos is Exalted by the Ruinous Powers, drawing the most avid worshippers of blood and carnage to his banner to wreak havoc upon the mortal realm. Though he spirals in a blood frenzy of his own making, Khargan is not without direction. He leads his warband against the forces of Order wherever they appear, and pledges himself to any cause that will lead him into the heart of violent slaughter.

Though the Fimir were long since abandoned by the malevolent gods of Chaos, the mysterious power of their Balefiend Sorcerers are still frequently used in the service of the Ruinous Powers. Among these Dark Magic-users, there are few more dedicated to the cause than Ketzak Fimdirach. A Balefiend of rare skill and intelligence, he is prophesised by the Meargh to restore greatness to the Fimir clans. Thus, a glorious destiny calls him forth on a quest of great importance to understanding the deepest arcane law of the word and wreak havoc in the name of his long-overlooked race.

With ambitions forged in the raging industrial furnaces of the Dark Lands, Ezar Doombolt is as determined and cruel as any Chaos Dwarf, willing to do anything to improve his standing among his peers. Driven by an unending greed, he forges a path built upon the backs of withered slaves and bloodied corpses. Though selfishness and disloyalty mark him as a most unreliable follower, he is not without reason. Promises of war-spoils and captives he can send back to Zharr-Naggrund to increase his own prestige are more than enough to secure his assistance... if only temporarily.

A bloodthirsty knight dedicated to the cause of Rot and Ruin, the Kurgan warrior Kayzk the Befouled has dedicated all to the service of Nurgle, Lord of Decay. The rotting pestilent mass that was once his flesh is untouched by pleasure or pain. Even should such feeling be possible, he could not give voice to it, for his vocal cords are no more than an open wound. Not even his soul remains to him, for it was offered to the Plaguefather as a trinket long ago. Now, Kayzk stands as nothing but a testament to the full horrors of Nurgle’s blessings.

The tight bonds among a pack of Werekin are severed only in death, leaving scars that never truly heal. Such are the wounds of Mournhowl, a ferocious and tragic figure among his tribe, who after the brutal slaughter of his kin now lets his grief echo through the night. With much of his tribe devoured by a Giant Jabberslythe named Skraelsbane, driven to madness and tainted by the Winds of Magic, Mournhowl alone leads the survivors in their quest for vengeance. With violent retribution in his heart, his powerful form stalks the land, vowing never to rest until the blood of his pack has finally been avenged.

Tamurkhan the Maggot Lord has been known by many names, each more vile and grotesque than the last. As a powerful Chaos Lord, and one of the greatest Kurgan Champions of Nurgle in recent history, his divine patron has blessed him with the ability to burrow into almost any host, taking control of their body as if he were its puppet master. Though his reeking maggot corpse has commandeered many faces, the Ogre Tyrant Karaka Breakmountain has become a favoured host. In such a powerful body, Tamurkhan now gathers his great horde, determined to fulfil a twisted prophecy that tells of a horrific reign of terror across the Chaos Wastes and beyond. Death and disease shall run rampant in the Bringer of Desolation's wake, for his hordes are seemingly endless and bent on destroying the world!

From the consumption of Plague victims to bathing in filth, nothing is beyond the unwholesome Pestigors of Nurgle. To face such creatures is a true assault on the senses, as well as one’s life – their dung-covered bodies are sparsely covered in fur that is matted and coarse, and riddled with myriad diseases of which they themselves are spared the symptoms due to their loyalty to Nurgle. Thus they retain the morbid vigour that characterises their master, their afflictions doing nothing to mar their battle-worthiness and savagery with a battle axe. The most favoured Pestigors are marked by their Tears of Nurgle: noxious secretions that ooze from their eyes, noses, ears and mouths, that they sputter upon their fleeing victims.

Plague Ogres have devolved in both mind, body and soul, their forms twisting and contorting into hellish shapes through the horrific blessings of Nurgle's Rot. When the Red Fist Tribe were defeated by Tamurkhan's horde, a great many Ogres submitted to his will and joined the monstrous host, from which point on they were lost to Chaos forever. Taking control of their Ogre Tyrant's body, Tamurkhan led them through foul rituals and the consumption of Chaos-tainted flesh, which sealed their fate. Soon, all manner of plagues and diseases were visited upon their desecrated bodies, their suffering only alleviated when they embraced Grandfather Nurgle fully. In battle, they slake their hunger and smash the foe in praise of the Lord of Decay – those that survived the Nurglish corruption, although many are barely recognisable as the Ogres they once were.

Trolls are hideous and malformed creatures, among whom a wide variety of different mutated sub-species and terrible deformities can be found. Perhaps the vilest examples are the Bile Trolls – cursed, tortured creatures with an appalling hunger that can never be satiated. It is said that their bloated and agonised forms endlessly regenerate like many Trolls, only to be digested by their own bilious innards again from within. Corrupt of flesh and dwelling in living agony, they receive no eventual respite from the horror of Father Nurgle’s influence, unlike many of His afflicted children. Furthermore, their stench lingers in the air as suspended droplets of bile that cause weapons to rapidly rust on the spot!

Toad Dragons are huge, reeking, primeval horrors. They are, for the fate of the world, blessedly few in number and confined largely to the trackless, otherworldly fens known as the Cold Mires under the coruscating skies of the uttermost north. These colossal beasts are near-mindless, violent and almost impossible to kill, and have a dire reputation in the legends of the Northern Wastes, which name them for their appearance and raw power. In truth they are perhaps far closer to the lumbering beasts that inhabit the jungles of Lustria than the true and ancient lineages of Dragon-kind.

The ability to spear a large monster from a distance or to skewer several man-sized creatures in a single shot appeals greatly to the violent and bloody nature of any Greenskin. The bolt thrower, or Bolt Throwa as it is termed by Orcs and Goblins, is a device commonly found in Greenskin armies. Working along the same lines as a giant crossbow, the device fires a single spear-sized bolt at high velocity. A well-placed shot can bring down a row of oncoming infantry, penetrate the armour of a steel-encased Knight or even slay an Ogre with a single shot – which is no easy feat given their considerable girth!

Gorbad Ironclaw is infamous even among other Orc Warbosses, rising to fame leading his tribe on countless successful Waaaghs! in his time. It was also he who first built Iron Rock, one of the most redoubtable Orc fortresses in the Old World. Conquering Greenskin tribes was never a real challenge for him either – it was his many, many horrific deeds in the Empire that saw him elevated to legendary status among his own kind, the name of Gorbad Ironclaw becoming an inspiration and a byword for "invasions done propa". Gorbad is immensely strong, even for an Orc. Despite his obvious brawn, he is known to win battles by using his head as well, fielding Goblins to effectively attack flanks or screen other troops' movements, and deploying massed archers, war machine batteries and other tactical advancements too. In short, Gorbad Ironclaw always drives whichever ragtag Greenskin host he is commanding, whether Orcs or Goblins they be, to do their utmost in the battle ahead.

Of Snagla's tribe, the Redvenom Forest Goblins, little is known. They were destroyed early on in the battles in the Drakwald, when men from the Empire first cut their frontiers deeper in to the surrounding forest. Snagla -- then one of the rising legends amongst the Forest Goblins along his band of Spider Riders, the Deff Creepers -- found his camp in ruins, and it is rumoured that then the Spider-god spoke to him. Snagla took the fangs from the his tribe's cannonball-blasted Arachnarok Spider, and with them fashioned a throwing spear and a great spiked club. With them, he has been at the forefront of every Greenskin victory, soaking the feathers of his distinct Redvenom garb in the blood of his enemies, and growing his legend.

The strange, improbable and often quite insane creatures known as Squigs are weird half-fungoid, half-flesh beasts that breed and multiply in symbiosis with the Greenskins. None of these match the sheer size of the Colossal Squig said to inhabit the depths of the Grey Mountains and the Vaults. These spherical monsters are of staggering size and possess insatiable appetites, no more in essence than an impossibly large, fleshy maw studded with row after row of scimitar-bladed teeth.

Ruglud's Armoured Orcs trace their lineage back to their founder’s strike of genius, never to be repeated, precipitated by a concurrent strike to the head by an oversized piece of masonry, as he was perusing the remains of a battle between Dwarfs and Chaos Dwarfs. Luckily, this happened while he was holding a crossbow and not, say, the bloody remains of a beard. And so Ruglud’s Armoured Orcs were formed, the only known band of Orcs to implement the combination of armour and crossbow. While disliked and distrusted by other Orc tribes, their fighting qualities are grudgingly accepted. Wherever the band travels, it fights for gold and food, and for the chance to strip the enemy of anything worth taking, including any crossbow ammo they can find.

Other Greenskins claim that living underground has driven Night Goblins mad, and it might be true. One thing is for certain: only the unhinged would try to catch a Great Cave Squig, and only absolute maniacs with little regard for life would dare chain together two Great Cave Squigs and then prod them towards the enemy. The ideal end result, from a Night Goblin's unconventional perspective, is that the Mangler Squigs enrage each other, whirling themselves into a tumbling motion. What follows is a spectacle of severed body parts and founts of gore, to the onlooking Night Goblins' delight.

Arbaal is one of the most devoted servants of Khorne, gifted with the power of the dreaded one-handed axe known as the Destroyer in recognition of his staunch devotion. Such a reward is not given to just any Champion, but one that has achieved much greatness and favour under the Blood God’s ever-leering gaze. To such Champions, however, also belongs Khorne's most uncompromising scrutiny. Should Arbaal falter, the magnitude of such a failure would cause him to lose all favour with the Blood God, rendering him as unremarkable amongst other Daemonic aberrations as he was remarkable in triumph, and perhaps worse. Over three thousand years of overwhelming battlefield dominance have made that prospect unthinkable, both for him and his enemies, whose wits literally fail them in searching for a way to bring him down.

As Skaramor tribesmen undertake the fated journey from Chaos Warriors to Wrathmongers, the Bloodspeakers chart their path, step by bloody step. The Pilgrimage of Skulls requires singular purpose quite apart from being willing to murder all in your path – though this is undoubtedly a requirement one absolutely cannot skirt, and also includes one’s fellow aspirants. The Bloodspeakers are there to provide and bolster that purpose. But what truly gives them their name and their place of high reverence in their tribe is their ability to call up otherworldly Daemonic horrors within the Brazen Cage’s pool of blood, a challenge that the aspirants must answer in a battle of a different kind.

Scyla Anfingrimm was once the bane of the coastlands from frozen Norsca to exotic Ind. A bloodthirsty raider and warrior-lord of the Ironpelt tribe, Scyla’s name was synonymous with victory and pillage, and all who met him saw the fire of a born leader in his eyes. By the end of Scyla’s second decade in the service of the Chaos Gods, he had become little more than a mountain of muscle and unquenchable rage, goaded into battle as a beast of war and unleashed to run howling into the ranks of the enemy. After Scyla’s subjugation of the troglodyte Gorgers that dwelt in the Undermountain, Khorne gifted his champion with the mind of a ravenous beast. His body flowed and spasmed out of control until his transformation into the mightiest Chaos Spawn in all the realms was complete.

From the moment he was strong enough to heft an axe, Skarr Bloodwrath swiftly garnered a reputation as a bloodthirsty butcher of the worst kind. Though his tribe did not deign to challenge the weak peoples of the south, Skarr found no shortage of foes to battle in Khorne’s honour. Unstoppable though he was, none could fight with such raging abandon without eventually being slain. Yet, his first death – and countless others after that – did not prove to be the end for this Champion of Khorne. Always has the Blood God brought him back to life through the spilled blood of his foes, so that Skarr may continue increasing his tally of skulls in return. Incessant resurrection has taken its toll, however, with the near-immortal warrior losing more of himself with each death, his grasp on reality slipping with each step on the road to Daemonhood.

The Skulltaker is the Blood God’s immortal champion, the greatest of all Khorne’s chosen Bloodletters. When not campaigning with his master’s armies, Skulltaker roams the Realm of Chaos at will atop his mighty Juggernaut, Kuhl’tyran. He appears before fortress and stronghold, drawn by tales of martial prowess and rumour of mighty combatants who might offer some small challenge. When a foe foolish and foolhardy enough emerges, Skulltaker dismounts from his loyal steed, salutes the enemy with upturned blade and charges forward to claim another skull in the Blood God’s name. Once only did he suffer defeat, at the hands of Sigmar. He still bears the scar he earned that day, and takes great pleasure in repaying the debt upon Sigmar’s inheritors at every given opportunity.

Bestigors are already some of the toughest of the Children of Chaos, yet even amongst them Khorngors are considered the most dangerous. Khorngors possess the great strength of their Bestigor brethren, but as might be expected from those marked by the God of Battle, they are far more vicious and quarrelsome and less able to restrain themselves from murderous excesses. With red-stained armour echoing the red skin of the Daemons of Khorne, they will eagerly slam into the front line of an enemy where other Bestigors might not hold their nerve. They are undoubtedly some of the most violent figures of all the obscene creatures to be found in any Daemonic horde.

The Northmen tribes of the Skaramor have long maintained an existence of constant battle throughout the Chaos Wastes. That they have rarely crossed the Sea of Chaos is a matter of choice; the Skaramor are devoted to claiming the skulls of the mightiest foes and offering them up to Khorne. The Skullreapers are the warrior-elite of the tribe, a blood-hungry caste even among a people feared for their wanton battle-lust. They are wrath and they are Ruin – howling, blood-mad reavers who fight and kill for the glory of Khorne. Few are they who can stand against them in battle, and countless are the skulls they have laid before the Skull Throne.

Amongst the Skullreapers of the mortal tribes there are those who stand apart, known by other Khorne-worshipping warriors as the Wrathmongers. They are feared and revered in equal measure, having braved a bloody path that few survive. Beginning their journeys under the tutelage of the Bloodspeakers, they are goaded into fighting amongst each other day and night and feed on the fallen. Finally, they undertake the Pilgrimage of Skulls to reach the Brazen Cage, the sacred Khornate shrine atop a mountain of skulls on the edge of the Realm of Chaos. There they battle Daemons summoned for the final trial, the stakes being the aspirants' own souls. Those who emerge alive are greater than when they entered, for their mortal flesh has been made mighty through battle and infused with the unnatural energies of slain Daemons.

Of all the cursed of Khorne, these creatures are at once the most twisted and brutal and yet most mysterious, for none can tell their true nature, whether they truly be Daemons or simply twisted, mutated mortals. The Bloodbeasts of Khorne are always masses of muscle and tendon, with pulsing veins and whip-cord sinew. Their every orifice is ringed with sharp teeth that tear into the flesh of those entangled within their elongated limbs. These limbs and tails are often armoured or scaled, while at their ends they transform into the shapes of crude but deadly weapons, flattening into blades and knives or bulging outwards into spiked maces. The Bloodbeasts are always hugely muscled, and are often emblazoned with the skull-mark of their Lord somewhere upon their bodies.

A Slaughterbrute is a hulking Chaos beast of muscle and aggression. Those among the forces of Chaos who seek to use such a beast for their own ends soon learn that such a mutant creature cannot be broken by conventional means, and those foolish enough to try are torn apart and eaten for their efforts. Instead, a Slaughterbrute's mind is enslaved, through sorcery, to that of a Chaos Champion. Though some Chaos Champions control a Slaughterbrute through the movement of a marionette, most are able to manipulate the creature through their own surpassing force of will – controlling its every action as if they were their own.

Ogres are a battle-hardened and fearless race, but there walks one amongst their number who is held in dread. Even veterans of a thousand battles feel corpulent shivers at the very name of this killer of killers, this shadowy figure that deals out the most gruesome kind of death imaginable. He is the champion executioner of Ogrekind, a slayer of kings and heroes. To see him on the field of battle is to see death itself at work. He is Bragg the Gutsman and none he has marked for slaughter have ever survived.

Aside from the Tyrant himself, a tribe's Bruisers are the most imposing Ogres in terms of sheer size and strength, and are often related to the kingdom's ruler. Bruisers spend a great deal of their time capitalising on their license to smack seven shades of dung out of any Ogre not toeing the line, not eating messily enough, or spending too much time playing with his Gnoblars. Bruisers are sometimes entrusted with the tribe's standard, a banner so robust it can be used as a weapon. A metal-bound pole smashed through one's head by a Bruiser will be felt no matter what's hanging from it.

More tales are told about Golgfag Maneater than any other Ogre alive, and Golgfag himself spins a great many of them. Yet there is much truth in the legend, for he has travelled the world far and wide with his cronies, imaginatively titled Golgfag’s Maneaters, with whom he has gained widespread notoriety as a battle-hardened mercenary leader. In truth, Golgfag’s adventures have won and lost him more fortunes than there are Gnoblars in the hills. His title ‘Maneater’ – coined when he once ate his human Paymaster whole and set off with his pay-chests – is a misleading moniker, for he is not picky at all about what he eats. Golgfag’s wanderlust may have prevented him from becoming a great leader up to now, but with enough loot and renown he may yet have his day!

Next to an Ogre army's cauldron, its paychest is probably amongst the most sacred of its possessions. It is usually entrusted to an Ogre most voluble, though not exactly valuable in terms of fighting skill. Being what they are, in the thick of combat Ogres may at times forget that gold awaits the ones who have distinguished themselves – which is why the Paymaster occupies a prominent place in their ranks and persists in extolling the virtues of the paychest with a single-mindedness that verges on mindlessness, both in and out of battle.

Ogre Maneaters are veterans of many campaigns fought in far-off lands. Travelling mercenaries without peer, they have spent decades accruing scars, tall tales, wealth and exotic wargear before heading back to the Ogre Kingdoms. Maneaters have fought throughout the Old World and beyond, and many races attempt to recruit such fighters into their armies, promising food, gold or whatever else the Ogres want in return for their services. The term ‘Maneater’ was originally coined for the mercenary captain Golgfag Maneater, after he ate his human Paymaster whole, but has become a general term for any Ogre who travels the land as a mercenary.

Being as well-travelled as the roaming Maneaters they serve, some Gnoblars have managed to acquire all sorts of clothing, weapons and strange customs on their travels. Among such customs is one of the Gnoblars’ most popular and dangerous sports picked up from Bretonnia, known as "pig jousting". Two Gnoblars sit across from each other on the backs of pigs and charge at each other in an attempt to unseat their opponents. When a Gnoblar horde goes to war, real pigs will not suffice in the intense circumstances of battle, so instead Gnoblars ride atop each other in a "piggy-back" manner using their "pig jousting" tactics to slay (or at least irritate) the enemy.

The Blood Vulture is a large, predatory bird that originates high in the Mountains of Mourn, belying its scavenging nature by having no qualms about using its sharp claws and powerful beak against living creatures. Given the gluttonous feeding frenzies in which the Ogres partake when they go to war, it is little wonder that they’ve developed a close relationship with the most vicious battlefield scavengers of the skies. Ogre Hunters in particular like to capture and tame Blood Vultures, using their deadly propensity for aggression to help them hunt down prey or attack their foes in battle.

Thundertusks are creatures of ice and doom, ancient monsters that strode the darkest ages long ago, when the world was frozen over. As it warmed, they drifted northwards, becoming imbued with the Winds of Magic, and turned into a physical manifestation of winter's chill. Thundertusks advance as relentlessly as a winter storm: a living engine of frozen destruction presaged by eldritch thunderclaps. Fierce predators, these creatures tower above most others in the mountains, although this doesn't stop ambitious Ogre tribes from attempting to capture and tame them. Once tamed, Thundertusks bring to bear their crushing bulk, freezing aura and blasts of magical ice in service of the Ogres.

The Yhetee packs inhabit the highest slopes of many mountain ranges, but are particularly common amongst the Mountains of Mourn and the place of their birth – the peaks of the Ancient Giant Holds. Though their iron-hard claws are the only weapon they require, a vestige of Ogre-like behaviour remains in the Yhetees’ ancestry to ensure that they still use clubs of a sort, an ice-weapon fashioned simply by snapping a bough from a tree and breathing pure cold onto it. It’s not uncommon for an Ogre tribe to include Yhetees amongst its ranks, though how or why the creatures are convinced to fight alongside Ogres is a subject of much speculation. A sense of kinship or a great debt owed from the distant past? Either way, when a Tyrant calls, they answer.

The more the servants of Slaanesh revel in their debased pleasures and refined iniquities, the closer they come to attaining special privilege in the eyes of their decadent God. While to other servants of Chaos, they may appear frivolously self-indulgent and even indolent, the Exalted Hero of Slaanesh’s physical senses and mental acuity are in fact so heightened that they react in the blink of an eye, and fight with blurring speed. While still prone to unpredictable whims and bouts of individuality, Slaanesh’s Exalted Heroes are among the greatest warriors in recorded history.

Sea Helms are the greatest heroes of Lothern, an order founded during the time of Bel Shanaar. With both spear and bow, they have perfected the quicksilver strike that cheats shields and parries to pierce throats, hearts and skulls.\\n\\nSea Helms often lead the ranks of Lothern Sea Guard, so that their presence may inspire others to greatness. The Sea Helm's finely-honed instincts combine with the Sea Guard's discipline to create a force that can swiftly adapt to changing fortunes.

Sea Lord Aislinn is a phenomenal tactician and an implacable foe. Under his control, the High Elf fleet has gained scores of impressive victories. While none question his successes, it has been noted that Lord Aislinn carries out his duties with ruthless enthusiasm and an air of viciousness that many in the courts of Ulthuan find distasteful.\\n\\nSnobbish and callous, the Sea Lord demonstrates the uglier side of the High Elves' notion that they are greater than all other races of the world. Aislinn has few qualms about starting wars in foreign lands if he in any way perceives it would benefit the High Elves' safety, status, or cause. Though he lacks popularity among Asur nobility, those under his command serve Aislinn with unquestionable loyalty and devotion.

As a seafaring race, the High Elves possess the most powerful navy in the world. The fleets of the Asur guard the coasts of Ulthuan, but they also range far and wide, sailing every ocean of the world and patrolling the sea lanes to ward against the enemies of the Elven people. Their ship crews are well-armed and far better trained than the sailors of other races, being especially proficient in hand-to-hand combat, and able to repel would-be boarders at sea or bolster High Elf forces during land battles if needed.

A Merwyrm is one of the most ancient creatures found in the seas of the Old World, being distant kin to the mighty winged Dragons. Loremasters believe Merwyrms once swarmed the primordial oceans of the Old World, but now they are rarely seen or heard of.\\n\\nAll Merwyrms possess long, almost serpentine bodies, covered in scales and corded with muscle, with four stubby limbs, each tipped with sharp claws. They lash their bodies to propel themselves through the deeps at great speed and possess a frightening gait across dry ground, adults being known to grow as large as a warship in length.

The Merwyrm Silak is said to be named after the old tales of a creature once bound by Kadon’s scroll. A huge beast that is part dragon and part sea-serpent, it is longer from horn to tail-tip than one of the great whales of the northern seas. It is dreaded as both a shipbreaker and a devourer, its bone-armoured maw wide enough to swallow most small barges in a single, devastating bite. When its colossal bulk rises out from the seas, it bellows a challenge that drowns out the din of battle before devouring foes like ants, swallowing up bodies, steel and screams into its gullet with indifferent and endless hunger.

Sea Elementals are living mountains of blue-black water that rear out of the sea in vaguely recognisable shapes, humanoid or bestial, and often with serpentine characteristics. They are immensely destructive, and have control over the seas around them, with the ability to summon raging storms, churning whirlpools, and battering hurricanes. Sea Elementals often fall upon their victims as a mighty deluge, sweeping them from the decks and sinking their ships.

Skycutters are sleek, airborne chariots held aloft by a cushion of magic. Drawn into battle by Swiftfeather Rocs, they serve as the eyes and ears of Lothern's mighty fleets, allowing engagements to be planned long before the enemy is even aware of their presence. Skycutters are also used as outriders for Lothern's armies, for they can go where their grounded kin cannot. Should a Skycutter's crew encounter a foe, their goal is to clear the skies, ensuring Lothern will dominate the heavens in the battle to come.

It is said that in ancient days, before even the Great Bastion was raised, or hammer-handed Sigmar rose in the verdant lands of the Reik, that there grew in the east beyond the Mountains of Mourn the immense empire of Kurgan. Only the best warriors were deemed worthy to recruit into the ranks of the Great Kurgan – the name by which their ruler was known, such was the mightiness of their domain. Their cruel dominion covered the vast steppe lands and ranged wide, marshalled in large part by their hordes of swift, versatile horsemen whose traditions have endured in the north into the present day.

In Ursfjord in the frozen north the great hall of Urslo is to be found. In this hall resides Beorg, chieftain of the Bearmen of Urslo, when he is not raiding or fighting. When Beorg, son of Bran, cracked the skulls of Uldsdau and Graill, twin sons of Huern, chieftain of the Tribe of the Wolf, the Chaos Gods chose to show their considerable favour. As Beorg threw himself upon his enemies, his back arched and split, his ribs cracked and turned in upon his body, and his face was consumed from within by a snarling black muzzle. The gift of the were was upon him, the gift of the Dark Gods to the people of Norsca. He was "Bearstruck."

Cyclopean fiends of mists and darkness, the Fimir are forsaken creatures of Chaos who live in seclusion in the Norscan wilderness. The civilised world has never been spared their aggressions, for across the ages they have sporadically appeared to raid isolated settlements of the Old World, and sometimes in cahoots with the Marauder hordes. Being amphibious bipeds of the bogs and fens, they appear as a brutish race of simple intelligence, but in reality there is a hierarchy in their fighting ranks. They are usually led by a Noble of their warrior-caste, though it is unclear whether such a leader arises due to his intellect. More likely their birth has some significance, or maybe they have simply proven themselves as one of the strongest warriors of their community.

Sayl the Faithless, infamous arch-sorcerer of the Dolgan tribe, is an utterly self-serving egotist and practiced murderer. A master of betrayal and treachery, never has he sworn allegiance to any single Ruinous Power, but rather paid lip service to many, pursuing pacts and bargains with petty Chaos godlings and Daemons, betraying each in turn when expedient, thus earning the epithet of ‘the Faithless’.\\n\\nWhile ostensibly in the service to the powerful Shaman-Sorcerer Schalkain the Vile, he goaded him into conducting a ritual which Sayl promptly sabotaged, murdering Schalkain and his other sorcerer-apprentices. Sayl, however was not untouched by his own treachery, his flesh mutating and his mortal sight lost to be replaced with hellish and maddening senses of the Daemon realm.

The Bearmen, like many of the tribes of Norsca, have been warped by their close contact with the Chaos Wastes. Given their ancestry, which some say stretches back to the Great Bear himself, their demeanour is unmistakably redolent of him. Few have truly pronounced ursine features unless looked upon from up close – at which point the observer is probably being torn apart or slashed to pieces. Though also known for their intermittent mercenary dealings with southerners, the Marauder Bearmen find straightforward raiding and pillaging vastly preferrable to conducting warfare on contract.

The three-headed Chimera is one of the most fearsome of all children of Chaos, a beast whose progenitors were so warped that it is now impossible to say what manner of creatures they might have been. Some scholars of the Old World have postulated that in times of magical dearth, Chimerae simply abandon the mortal plane altogether, to instead hunt prey through the rich and sorcerous fields of the Realm of Chaos. Others believe that Chimerae are not creatures of flesh and blood at all, but rather monsters called into being only when the Winds of Magic are at their most fulsome -- savage emissaries sent by the darkest of the Dark Gods.

Even amid the troll-haunted, Chaos-tainted wastes of Norsca, few creatures are as feared and hated as the Curs’d Ettin. Renowned in dread Norscan saga and tale, the twin-headed Curs’d are terrors of the high moorlands and mountains of the Northlands, dwelling in lonely caverns and forlorn and shattered fortresses, daubed in the blood of their former owners. Hulking, twisted creatures, these towering monstrosities are easily distinguished from the more commonplace lumbering giants of the Old World by their singular deformities and their cruel intellect, although they share both their size and great hunger for flesh.

Dwelling in the mires of tainted sludge and ooze that stretch across vast areas of the Chaos Wastes, Dread Maws are one of the vilest creatures to have emerged from these blighted lands. The first sign of their presence is an ominous rumbling from beneath the ground as the Dread Maws grind and chew their way through the earth, swiftly followed by an eruption of mud and the stench of putrid slime as their gaping jaws burst forth. Any warriors brave enough to assault them will have their weapons fouled and limbs caught in the vile substances exuded by the Maw, which is almost impossible to hack through.

Even wilder and crueller than others of their kin, these Daemonette huntresses afflict their victims with the poisonous horror of their claws and their steeds' obscene aspect. Pleasureseekers savage yearning for pleasure is such that it takes no more than a split-second for them to overwhelm their foes. Even those who survive the encounter are rendered insane by hallucinatory sensations both terrifying and wondrous – the more the quarry tries to banish them from their thoughts, the more hungrily the Pleasureseekers lust after them.

Dechala is the mistress of the Tormentors, the greatest of all Slaanesh’s warbands to ever roam the Chaos Wastes. She is as cruel as she is beautiful and as pitiless as she is beguiling. Grasping a sword in each of her multitudinous hands, her approach promises terrible pain and pleasure to any who dare stand before her.\\n\\nDechala seeks the ultimate self-indulgence and freedom from the shackles of law and order, but desires this pleasure only for herself: others can suffer as long as her wishes are fulfilled. She is served by a host of Thralls, victims of her hideous endeavours that erode both will and body.

The Masque of Slaanesh was once the Daemonette held in the greatest regard by Slaanesh for her dancing skill. It, too, is what doomed her, as He perceived a slight where there was none in her attempt to soothe him with a performance following a terrible defeat.\\n\\nThe power of the Masque's curse – to dance endlessly, enacting Slaanesh's story, past and future – allows her to recreate events as far back as her God's birth, as well as those yet to come. Any who survive these visceral manifestations are left with but the scantest memories of what truly occurred, seeing only the Ruin and death around them, and feeling only the bone-weary agony of a body pushed beyond its limits. Meanwhile and elsewhere, the Masque dances on...

Born into the Sortsvinaer tribe on the northern coast of Norsca, Styrkaar succeeded his father Jerg Svengor as leader of the tribe after killing him in a duel instigated by Styrkaar's constant secret companion since childhood – a Daemonic spirit of Slaanesh. In his meteoric rise to fame, Styrkaar laid low many of the famed warlords of the Chaos Wastes, including champions of his own God. Having proved his mettle on the field and his willingness to go to unheard-of lengths in celebrating each victory, Styrkaar became a favoured lieutenant of Archaon himself!

The Cult of Slaanesh amongst the Dark Elves began as part of Morathi's bid for power over Naggaroth’s northern invaders from the Chaos Wastes. As it was superseded by the worship of Khaine, many believed it had been suppressed. However, the Cult had gathered devotees so unflinching in their faith that many outright considered themselves belonging to the Dark Prince rather than under the rule of the Druchii. Marked by His favour and bolstered by their tenacity, they are always ready to clear the path for Slaanesh’s more powerful servants.

The Beastmen most ostensibly devoted to the Dark Prince often have a goat-like face and horns, qualities known to be flavoured by their master. What is most prevalent in them, however, is the gluttonous excesses they indulge in as part of their worship, which are as much a part of their bestial nature as blood and pain. Their appearance is one of brutes in pastel-shaded fur – sometimes painstakingly dyed – with horns elaborately curved in the rune-symbol of Slaanesh. They take inordinate pleasure in being on the receiving end of fierce charges, whipping the foolhardy aggressors for their audacity.

Some devoted followers of Slaanesh begin to falter in their faith once the Dark Prince begins to bestow His unwholesome gifts upon them, whereas others bathe openly in what sets them apart from lesser mortals, and so truly come into their own – and step beyond the point of salvation. Such explorers leave behind all remnants of their humanity and set upon an endless quest for the ultimate sensation and self-indulgence. Freed, or trapped, in this existence, depending on your point of view, they consider every other creature to be subservient to their will. They will obey them... adore them, or be destroyed!

Dark legend has it that this terrible hatred was born long ago when Beastmen Bray-Shamans created the first Preytons in horrific rituals, corrupting Great Stags before their sacrifice-strewn herdstones. Bereft of their once noble nature Preytons now know only an all-encompassing hatred for that which they have lost, driving them to rend and kill with terrible malice. Corpses mauled beyond recognition and stretches of forest befouled and trampled betray their presence. Anything foolish enough to enter such an area will be hunted down and slain, and often the Preytons will simply discard the torn corpse to rot, killing out of pure hatred, rather than hunger.

In the long distant past, at the time of the Sundering, many Druchii under the influence of Morathi turned to the worship of Slaanesh. As catastrophic civil war erupted, some favoured warriors who had dedicated their souls to the Dark Prince were gifted with fell, unnatural powers. When the Cult was outlawed and replaced with the worship of Khaine, these favourites of Slaanesh hid themselves from prying eyes, though some journeyed to the far north, there to meet battle with the denizens of the Chaos Realms and experience every sensation possible. As millennia passed, the numbers of these now supremely powerful beings, known as the Anointed, dwindled, so that only a handful remain.

The priests of ancient Nehekhara taught that upon death, the spirit travelled to the Underworld – the fabled Realm of Souls. However, those unworthy of the golden paradise awaiting there cast down into the lower depths, to be hunted and devoured by the Hounds of Usirian – the Dread Abyssals.\\nAs Nagash turned Nehekhara into a realm of the undead, the Underworld was parched of souls, and the Dread Abyssals paced like caged beasts, growing hungrier and hungrier for souls. It is this hunger and the thinning boundary between the world of the living and the dead that made possible for mighty necromancers to lure the Dread Abyssals forth to serve as steeds.

The loud, brash Knights of the White Wolf follow the creed of their patron Ulric both in deed and demeanour. They are amongst the most numerous and powerful of all Knightly Orders in the Empire, especially strong around Middenheim where the Order was created to combat the forces of Chaos on equal footing and protect the city from harm. Keeping alive the old fierce ways of their warrior forebears, they wear mantles of wolf skin over their armour, and spurn shields, helms and lances in favour of heavy two-handed war hammers. Swinging their weapons around their heads, they knock enemy horsemen from their saddles and pound the skulls of enemy foot troops.

To be a Knight of the White Wolf is to cleave to a fierce, ancient tradition markedly different than that of most other knightly Orders, and the Fellwolf Brotherhood is the epitome of that. Considered the most ill-disciplined of the Order, they believe their actions must speak louder than their sometimes-questionable words. Nevertheless, their brand of howling savagery makes them Middenheim’s biggest asset, being deployed at times to protect the city against similarly savage invaders. In battle, the Brotherhood are in their element and that of Ulric. They ask for no recognition but that granted by their own and pursue no higher station other than being the mighty weapons of war that they are.

The Knights Panther are a formal Order that traces its origins to the crusades against Araby. When the returning crusaders brought back the pelts of outlandish animals, they hung them from the pauldrons of their armour as trophies of their bloody victories. Thus was born the Order of the Knights Panther, a courageous brotherhood that is known and respected throughout the Empire. Their mastery of battle tactics more than compensates for their unconventional attire, for in their grasp of war, they are one of the most powerful martial forces the Empire can offer.

Many soldiers of Middenheim are followers of the Winter God and take part in campaigns with his name on their lips. But it is the current Ar-Ulric, Emil Valgeir, who unites them all in religous purpose, no matter their training. He alone wields enough sway in matters both spiritual and material to act as the very soul of such an army, as his title proclaims. Though Priests of Ulric are required to follow martial pursuits as a matter of course, there are few as fierce as Valgeir, despite his age. His Hammer-axe of Skoll and his Wolfplate Armour are as much vestments of war as they are symbols of his religious office.

In Middenland, like nowhere else in the Empire, Sigmar falls second in worship to one of the Old Gods: Ulric, the Wolf God of Winter. Life in the northern Empire is harsh; winters are freezing, the soil is poor, and the forests crawl with Goblins and Beastmen. Ulric is as harsh as the land itself, demanding strength and independence from his followers to harden them to the austerity of their existence. Ulric's warrior Priests reflect this quality, forbidden to enter the cult if they do not follow a martial pursuit themselves. In their faith and actions on the battlefield they confront problems head-on and by force of arms whenever possible, embodying Ulric’s spirit as they swing their weapons and bellow oaths to their enemies.

Seneschals are hardened veterans of the Knights of the White Wolf, a Knightly Order based in Middenheim devoted to the Cult of Ulric, the God of Winter. Unlike a Grand Master, who leads the Order’s battalions into the fray, a Seneschal of the White Wolf might be found at the helm of any Empire army, embodying their cult’s tenets of directness, bravery and force of arms. They are amongst the most fearless and fiercest of leaders, elevating themselves into command through numerous displays of strength and fortitude. They will have spearheaded and survived countless wild charges at their armies’ helms, bellowing savage oaths to Ulric in guttural howls that send the Empire’s foes flying even before the final impact of their charges.

The Drakwald Forest is vast and treacherous, and many monstrosities make their lairs deep within it. Such creatures must be purged from time to time lest their numbers grow out of control. Finding their lairs is notoriously difficult, so Middenlanders use packs of hounds to sniff them out and help hunt them down, whether by signalling the presence of a creature to be killed or doing it themselves. Once prompted by their handlers, they make up for their single-mindedness in speed and instinctive savagery.

The Teutogen Guard are the personal bodyguard of Ar-Ulric – the High Priest of Ulric – accompanying him both at state occasions and on the battlefield. Named after the great Teutogen tribe that helped the man-god Sigmar drive the Orc and Goblin invaders from the lands of men, they are selected from the ranks of the Templars of Ulric – the Knights of the White Wolf. Each year the Guard is renewed, its new members selected by the Grand Master of the Order and Ar-Ulric himself. Inductees are often taken from the Inner Circle, although the selection process takes account of merit rather than rank, allowing ordinary brethren to be just as likely chosen for the preeminent honour.

Ulric is the God of Warriors across the Old World, and initiates of his cult are expected to make their way in the world by directness, bravery, and force of arms. A good number find their calling in formal armies and mercenary regiments, yet in the Empire there are many wandering fighters seeking adventure, fortune, or simply to honour their patron. When Ar-Ulric announces a holy campaign, many of these warriors heed the call, and those that are able make their way to Middenheim to take up the cause. They band together in groups of like-minded souls, frequently using tests of arms to establish leaders and standard-bearers amongst them.

The Wolf-kin are fighters driven to near-madness by hardship and despair. Rather than lower themselves to morose preaching or punishment for Man's sins and the end of the world, however, followers of Ulric traumatised in this way take a more direct approach befitting their pragmatic and vengeful god. Gathering together, they travel the roads and forests seeking out Beastmen, Orcs, and evil in any form. Though often sombre and quick to anger, the warriors of the Wolf-kin are welcomed into Middenland's armies, for their bravery and power more than make up for their impetuousness.

In times of desperate need, when the signs and portents indicate the fate of the Empire itself lies in the balance, the Patriarch of the Celestial Order may eschew subtlety and sanction the use of one of his Order's largest and most destructive weapons – a Celestial Hurricanum. These battle altars were originally built to help Celestial Wizards in their studies of the heavens and aid them in making more accurate predictions of the future. At the heart of each Hurricanum lies a treasured artifact – one of Teclis’ Orbs of Sorcery, which enables them to do more than just observe the orbits of passing comets; they actually alter their paths and cause them to come crashing down from the heavens.

Long ago, the Liche Priests of Nehekhara used their accumulated knowledge to trap their own souls within their bodies, and in doing so they extended their lives far beyond those of mortal men. However, whilst their spirits never passed into the Realm of Souls, their bodies have withered with the passing of centuries, and it is their spirit alone that now animates their forms. Without realising it, the entire priesthood cursed itself – not to eternal life, but to eternal Undeath, and servitude to their kings. Though none of them can escape their unending responsibilities, some are allowed a modicum of power and control over enacting their masters' will.

A Tomb Herald is a Tomb King's personal champion and most trusted bodyguard. They stand between their king and any danger coming his way, heedless of their own safety. And when the moment comes for a Tomb King to die, so must the Herald, to protect his master's deathless soul. Thus, when the Tomb King awakens from his sarcophagus, his most loyal retainer is already standing at his side, ready to slay his liege-lord's foes and enforce his will over the lands once more. When that will calls for spreading the king's mandate, the Tomb Herald acts as his master's voice. When it calls for destruction, the Tomb Herald acts as the sword that lays low his foes.

Beneath the shifting, endless Sands of Nehekhara dwell age-old secrets and timeless horrors to freeze the soul of any who dare disturb their slumber. Many are the legends and whispered tales that are gathered about them, one of the most fabled and feared being of the gigantic scarabs and carrion-beetles said to dwell in the dunes. Known to the loremasters of Tilea and the Empire as Khemric Titans, these giant arcane constructs of stone and onyx, bejewelled and enamelled with the wealth and glory of a bygone age, tower above even the dreaded Necrosphinx in size, animated by the mightiest incantations of the fallen glory of the south.

The Ushabti guard of Nagash's inner sanctum, the Sepulchrex respond only to the Great Necromancer’s will. Even Arkhan the Black, trusted though he was, had no control over their actions. Many of the Nehekharan kings thought it strange that Nagash would surround himself with graven images of the gods he had cast down, but Mannfred von Carstein, himself no stranger to hubris, had grasped the truth of the matter. The Sepulchrex bore the gods' likenesses precisely because Nagash had defeated them. They were reminders of a cherished victory, their voiceless servitude one of the Great Necromancer's few remaining conceits.

At first glance, it could be said that Bloab Rotspawned is surrounded by swarms of flying insects. But in truth, Bloab [[i]]is[[/i]] the swarm, and the swarm is Bloab. Once a tall and athletic warrior, now his mortal form is naught but a sack of leathery skin filled with writhing Daemon-maggots. His youth was spent in cruel fascination with the smaller creatures, sadistically torturing and killing them. But Nurgle took offense to this meaningless cessation of life, and one night, as he slept, Bloab was visited by a swarm of Daemon Flies. First one, then a second, then a writhing cloud forced its way down his throat. Laying eggs throughout his body, they left him asleep still. Soon, the eggs hatched, and the creatures began to eat him alive, the smaller creatures visiting revenge from within. Since that night, Nurgle has come to favour Bloab and his wretched form, even granting him rare access to his vibrant garden.

The three brothers, Ethrac, Otto and Ghurk Glott, were born in Norsca to two Empire citizens, Ethra and Ollos, peaceful folk who sought to break the cycle of violent warfare around them. Upon arrival, Ethra soon fell pregnant with triplets, her belly swelling to a prodigious size. A Norscan hag, jealous of Ethra, cut her with a rusted knife. The wound festered, and Ethra called out to the gods to save her. Father Nurgle listened, and soon after, three children were born.\\n\\nEthrac took after his mother, a magic user and a quick study. Otto assisted his father with the harvest, swinging his great scythe with commanding strength. Ghurk proved wayward, preferring to brawl and chase women. With the Glott parents unable to stop the Norscans from their raiding way of life, a reprisal force from Nordland arrived on the shores of Norsca. Ethra and Ollos’ deaths by Nordland’s halberdiers would see the brothers cry out for vengeance and embrace Father Nurgle’s gifts. As the favour of their foul patron grows in the Befouled Brothers' host, their vengeance may yet be realised.

Gutrot Spume is the Lord of Tentacles and the Master of the Plague fleets. From his youth, his arrogance led him to dive into the frigid waters of the Sea of Claws with only a knife, eventually returning with dead eater-fish and swordsharks that prowled those waters. His successes were noted and recognised by senior members of the Dragonbone tribe, but it was not they he sought to impress, but the gods. His prey grew ever more ambitious, ever deadlier, until he, along with a flotilla of warships he had amassed, hunted down a rot-kraken haunting the coast. Diving into the water, he fought fiercely, but was overwhelmed by smaller tentacled foes. That should have been his end, but the Urfather felt generous that day, and spared his life. He returned changed, one arm replaced with a tentacle, his gut swollen, and his skin the ghostly white of an undersea beast.

During his troubled birth, Morbidex's Norscan village has been burnt down. Disfigured by the flames, his appearance was fearsome to all who beheld it. Yet it was his martial skill that gained him recognition – then authority – within his tribe. A lifelong worshipper of the Dark Gods, Morbidex believed that the flames that disfigured him were caused by Tzeentch, and vowed to take revenge by first gaining Nurgle's aid. Against advice, he travelled north, seeking the Realms of Chaos. In the end, the Garden of Nurgle came to him in the form of an avalanche of giggling, excited Nurglings. Promising their aid, the Nurglings began to speak riddles. For those answered correctly, he received assistance. For those incorrect, his form was altered to mimic the Nurglings. From one error, his belly distended, from another, his face became a Nurgling's hideous grin. Thus was Morbidex given the name: Twiceborn.

Orghotts' one and only desire is to become a true Daemon. The locals of the Icehorn tribe whisper that Orghotts, some centuries old by this time, was born of the union between a Great Unclean One and a human witch, though the details are fortunately unclear. Orghotts himself is resentful that he must endure the mortal realm, wishing to reside instead in the Garden of Nurgle. His weapons, two rot-bladed axes, were found when the slopes of the Icehorn mountains and the realm of Chaos merged during the ebb and flow of the Chaos energies. He desires only to return to the Garden of Nurgle, but to do that he must prove himself or contract Nurgle's Rot. He has tried both, but this glory still eludes him.

The sane shrink from contagion in all its forms, but those who become favoured by the Plague Lord are far from sane. When one becomes Nurgle’s Chosen, His mark appears on the body as three circular lesions, typically weeping poisonous pus or infested with wriggling maggots. Despite this perceived displeasure, it is a blemish sought by and reserved for His most loyal servants. Most individuals develop a supernatural tolerance to pain, despite their festering flesh, allowing them to enjoy the slow degeneration without distraction. They also become inured to battle wounds, making it very difficult to slay them – some have to be chopped to pieces before they die.

The Flayerkin are horrifying, twisted mutants, forged from a fusion of Chaos Marauder flesh and hell-forged iron. Many marauders are sent to undergo this process by their sadistic masters, but some seek it out through unbridled insanity. The Skaven themselves perform these modifications, grafting weapons onto crudely-amputated limbs. Some are given hooks, some claws, some are given deadly, barbed blades to behead the enemies of Chaos with their wild, heedless swings.

The great powers of Chaos have mutated many a creature, some to suit their will, others through sheer happenstance. This beast appears to be the latter, though the whims of the Chaos gods are not so easily deciphered. The flesh of these beasts has swollen near to bursting, its flesh torn in places, either by rapidly growing muscle, or by a thick, sharp spike protruding from the skin. In constant pain, these beasts can find brief relief only in the act of killing, a task they seek out constantly.

The Putrid Blightkings' number are made of those touched by Nurgle, through his emissaries hatched from the Sorcerer Lord Bloab Rotspawned. These flies leave their host, in search of warriors that have proven themselves worthy of Nurgle's favour. A single bite, and the boons of Nurgle – great strength and resilience – are granted to the faithful. These warriors act as bodyguards to the Urfather's Champions, attuned to his whims and desires completely. They are selected for glory, but above all, they are given destiny. They are the killers that bring the mighty and the monstrous low, to ensure that the cycle of life and death remains unbroken.

Found in the most treacherous regions of the world, from the Bloodspine Mountains to the Grey Peaks that border the Empire, Basilisks are a living blight that can swiftly reduce an area to a ruinous wasteland. Despite their reclusive nature, they are incredibly deadly, using their poisonous aura to clear nearby plantlife, before lunging at their prey with deadly speed. Their gaze, as well, carries the same withering nature as their aura. Those that a Basilisks' gaze falls upon feel their flesh and mind unravel as one.

The Chaos Dwarfs have long regarded the giants as a potential weapon of war, large as they are. But true to their nature, they believed they could improve upon the existing creature. So they began, mutilating these creatures in a variety of grim and deliberate ways. Limbs were hacked away, giant metal hooks and claws bolted to bone in their place. Thick plates of armour, fitted to their form in places, hammered into the flesh in others. The result is a creature even more clumsy and unwieldy, but one that can shrug off far more bullets and arrows than before.
As dangerous as tehy are preatty, skeleton 5 are a force to ber 3eckoned with.

Long thought by some to have been stolen from the temple of Nurgle, the Plague God of Chaos, before being reconsecrated to the Hornet Rat at the very beginning of time, others consider the Cauldron a Lizardman artefact, taken far more recently by Clan Pestilens from among the ruins of a temple-city in Lustria.\\n\\nIn battle, the Plague Priests ensure each Cauldron carries one of the Seven Lethal Poxes for use in war – maladies so unstable and so deadly they may even infect other Skaven troops in their vicinity – for the glory of the Horned Rat, of course.

When the Horned Rat relented and released the long-imprisoned Council of Thirteen from the black pit into which he had cast them, what emerged was more than a mere mass of foul melded rat-flesh. A further blast of black lightning gave the Verminlord its final, hideous mortal form. Anointing the Rat Daemon with a belch of his own godly power, the Horned Rat had created Skreech Verminking, the greatest of his kind.\\n\\nImbued with the sneaky stealth of a Clan Eshin assassin, the Grey Seers’ arcane skillset, Clan Skryre’s insights into technology, Clan Moulder’s ability to craft flesh itself, the martial ambition and battle-lust of the Warrior Clans, and a deep knowledge of the foulest diseases imaginable, Skreech, also known as the Rat King, has pledged to spread the vilest corruption in the Horned Rat’s cursed name.

That innate Skaven talent for treachery and greed is strong in Thanquol’s veins. In fact, even by their low standards, the Ascendant Grey Seer has never missed an opportunity to benefit himself, especially at the expense of anyone and everyone else. He also has the luck of the Horned Rat himself, somehow extricating himself from the wildest of fixes with two rat-like feet planted firmly on the ground and the favour of the Council intact.\\n\\nIn his lengthy career, Thanquol has commanded armies, led espionage campaigns, hunted for sacred artefacts, and fostered rebellion among the many enemies of the Skaven race. Alongside him almost always has been Boneripper, his loyal Rat-Ogre mount. With the favour of the greatest Daemon Verminlord, Skreech Verminking, Thanquol’s Masterplans will surely sooner or later come to verminous fruition to the detriment of his hapless foes.

Verminlord Corruptors are the Daemonic embodiment of pestilence, constantly mired in a miasma of sickness that causes nearby life to immediately wither away. They exist to spread disease throughout the mortal realm, and are most likely to be found striding among the frontlines, goading their Skaven servants to greater violence and calling plaguestorms whilst vomiting poisonous fountains.\\n\\nAnything close to a Corruptor faces the teeming mass of foul parasites infesting their pelt, and a bite from the Verminlord transmitting bubonix and causing rot within minutes. The Corruptor will then summon forth twin Plaguereapers to dice the foe into bloody, diseased pieces.

Verminlord Deceivers are known colloquially as “Shadows That Kill”.
